newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK utilities buoyant despite Budget tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK utilities buoyant despite Budget tax.

text.p: British utility stocks leapt on Tuesday as confidence was buoyed by Severn Trent's promise to give cash to shareholders, despite the government's call for a review of regulation and the shadow of a tax on excess profits.
"The timing of Severn Trent's announcement exudes confidence, so the sentiment out there is buoyant," said one sector analyst.
Severn Trent said on Monday that it would complete a 10 percent buyback of shares having bought 5.6 percent in December.
That promise came on the same day that Trade and Industry Secretary for the new centre-left Labour government Margaret Beckett launched a review of regulation.
On Wednesday, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown should give details of a one-off tax on excess profits of privatised utilities in his first Budget.

But share prices were sharply higher on Tuesday as the market saw Severn Trent's move as a possible precursor to further benefits for shareholders and felt the government's tough line on utilities might be easing.
"The windfall tax is largely factored in and there was nothing that was at all worrying in the announcement of the regulatory review," the analyst said.
A total levy of around five billion pounds ($8.3 billion) for the so-called "windfall" tax is widely expected and share prices have adjusted accordingly, analysts said.

Wessex Water, which has one of the lowest debt profiles of the sector, had jumped 26-1/2 pence by 1110 GMT to 430 pence while Thames Water, which has said it will seek shareholder approval to buy back shares, gained 15 pence to 708.5 pence.
Among electricity stocks, Scottish Power rose 17-1/2 pence to 408-1/2 pence and generator National Power added 16-1/2 pence to 538-1/2.
"Beckett's comments appeared slightly resassuring, more conciliatory, so the market has taken that as positive in a non-negative way," the analyst said.
The share-watching Financial Times Lex column said on Tuesday that there were signs of a "striking" change of rhetoric from Beckett in her announcement of the review.
It said she appeared to be taking a less populist line against the profits made by utilities and that she appeared set on creating a long-term stable framework for companies.
"Utilities can look forward to less risk, a lower cost of capital and maybe higher valuations" once the windfall tax is dealt with, the Financial Times said.
Beckett ruled out any switch to rate-of-return regulation from current formulae based on inflation to cap prices, and said she did not feel executive pay was a prime consideration for the review.
She said the inter-departmental review was expected to produce a report by the end of the year and if changes were recommended, a consultation paper would then be issued.
"It's a long-term debate, there are not going to be any swift changes and the focus seems to be on the structure of regulatory institutions, not regulation itself," the analyst said.

Labour has been fiercely critical of the utilities which were privatised by previous Conservative administrations for hefty shareholder payouts and fat executive pay packets while it claimed customers were losing out.
Water companies in particular have been lashed after the hot summer of 1995 saw many imposing curbs on domestic demand while allowing over 800 million gallons of supplies to seep out of pipes daily.
The government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, called a crisis summit in mid-May as the drought, Britain's worst for 200 years, dragged on.
It laid out a 10-point plan for water companies including mandatory targets for cutting leaks. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
